title: Board-pattern readiness test — most-repeated question types
chapter: CBSE Class 10 Mathematics · Chapter 1 Real Numbers (NCERT reprint 2026-27)
tagline: Practice questions modelled on past CBSE papers; not predictions of this year's paper.
disclaimer: Original questions modelled on question types that have repeated in CBSE board papers 2023-2026 and the Sample Question Papers 2024-25 to 2026-27. They are practice for readiness, not predictions of what will appear in any exam.
instructions: 40 questions. MCQ and assertion-reason: choose one option. Numeric: type a whole number (negative allowed). No calculator.

patterns.T8: Unknown power / factor in a factorisation

S1.name: Primes, composites and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
S1.tip: Learn the exact FTA wording: every composite number is a product of primes, unique apart from order. Remember 1 is neither prime nor composite.

S2.name: Prime factorisation
S2.tip: Divide by the smallest prime again and again, then write the answer in index form (2³ × 3² …). Test primes only up to √n.

S3.name: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
S3.tip: HCF = smallest power of each common prime; LCM = greatest power of every prime that appears. Line the factorisations up in columns.
S3.ncert: NCERT Examples 2 and 4; Exercise 1.1 Q2, Q3

S4.name: HCF × LCM = product and HCF/LCM properties
S4.tip: HCF × LCM = product holds for two numbers only. The HCF must always divide the LCM.
S4.ncert: NCERT Example 3 and the Remark after Example 4; Exercise 1.1 Q2, Q4

S5.name: HCF/LCM word problems (incl. remainders)
S5.tip: Clue words: 'largest / greatest that divides' → HCF; 'together again / least number divisible' → LCM. With remainders, subtract first (HCF) or add after (LCM).
S5.ncert: NCERT Exercise 1.1 Q7; then past-paper word problems

S6.name: kⁿ ending in 0 and composite numbers
S6.tip: A number ends in 0 only if its prime factorisation has both 2 and 5. For 'composite' checks, take out the common factor.

S7.name: Irrational numbers: definition and closure facts
S7.tip: Irrational = cannot be written as p/q. Rational ± irrational is irrational, but two irrationals can add or multiply to a rational.

S8.name: Proof that √p is irrational
S8.tip: Write the proof in steps: assume √p = a/b with a, b coprime; square; use 'p divides a² ⇒ p divides a' (p prime); reach the contradiction.
S8.ncert: NCERT Theorems 1.2, 1.3 and Example 5; Exercise 1.2 Q1

S9.name: Proving a ± b√p, 1/√p irrational
S9.tip: Assume the number is a/b, isolate the root on one side, and show the other side is rational, which contradicts the known irrational root.

S10.name: Unknown powers in a factorisation
S10.tip: Factorise the given number completely, then match the powers term by term. For LCM conditions, the greatest power wins.
S10.ncert: Practise index form with NCERT Exercise 1.1 Q1, Q3 (past-paper type, no direct NCERT question)

S11.name: HCF written as a combination
S11.tip: Find the HCF by prime factorisation first, then substitute and solve the simple equation for the unknown.
S11.ncert: Past-paper type; no direct NCERT exercise. Revise HCF (Exercise 1.1 Q2) first

questions.question: Which of these numbers is neither prime nor composite?
questions.explanation: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime (exactly two factors) nor composite (more than two).

questions.explanation: FTA: every composite is a product of primes in exactly one way, ignoring order.

unique, including the order of the factors

questions.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 4 and their LCM is 240. Find their HCF.
questions.explanation: Numbers 3x and 4x; LCM = 12x = 240, so x = 20 = HCF.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: ratio trick.

questions.question: For the numbers 8, 12 and 18, which statement is true?
questions.explanation: HCF = 2, LCM = 72, so HCF × LCM = 144 ≠ 1728. The product rule is for two numbers only.
questions.remediation: Video part 4 'Careful' card; worksheet notes 4.
options: HCF × LCM = 144, which is not equal to the product 1728

questions.question: Find the smallest 4-digit number that is exactly divisible by 12, 18 and 30.
questions.explanation: LCM = 180. 1000 ÷ 180 ≈ 5.56, so the next multiple is 6 × 180 = 1080.

questions.question: Which of these numbers is composite?
questions.explanation: 3 × 5 × 7 + 7 = 7 × 16 = 112. The '+1' numbers are 211, 31 and 7, all prime: a product plus 1 is not automatically composite.

questions.question: The first step in proving that √7 is irrational is:
questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction starts by assuming the number is rational in lowest terms.

options: Assume √7 = a/b, where a, b are coprime integers and b ≠ 0

questions.question: In the proof that √3 is irrational, from 3b² = a² we conclude:
questions.explanation: 3 divides a², and since 3 is prime, 3 divides a (theorem: p prime, p | a² ⇒ p | a).
questions.remediation: Video parts 7 and 9: quote the prime theorem, not 'even/odd'.

questions.question: A student copies the √p proof to 'prove' √9 is irrational. Which step fails?
questions.explanation: The theorem needs a prime. Counterexample: a = 3, a² = 9 is divisible by 9 but a is not. Indeed √9 = 3 is rational.
questions.remediation: Video part 9, 'the proof needs a prime'.
options: Assuming a and b are coprime
Concluding '9 divides a' from '9 divides a²', because 9 is not prime
